title: Isaiah 19 — The oracle concerning Egypt: YHWH on a swift cloud, the Nile dried up, and the altar in the land of Egypt

paragraphs.text: מַשָּׂ֖א מִצְרָ֑יִם הִנֵּ֨ה יְהוָ֜ה רֹכֵ֨ב עַל־עָ֥ב קַל֙ וּבָ֣א מִצְרַ֔יִם וְנָע֞וּ אֱלִילֵ֤י מִצְרַ֙יִם֙ מִפָּנָ֔יו וּלְבַ֥ב מִצְרַ֖יִם יִמַּ֥ס בְּקִרְבּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: The oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, YHWH rides on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt shall tremble before him, and the heart of Egypt shall melt within it.
i18n.he: מַשָּׂ֖א מִצְרָ֑יִם הִנֵּ֨ה יְהוָ֜ה רֹכֵ֨ב עַל־עָ֥ב קַל֙ וּבָ֣א מִצְרַ֔יִם וְנָע֞וּ אֱלִילֵ֤י מִצְרַ֙יִם֙ מִפָּנָ֔יו וּלְבַ֥ב מִצְרַ֖יִם יִמַּ֥ס בְּקִרְבּֽוֹ׃

notes.official:
*Rōḵēḇ ʿal-ʿāḇ qal* “rides on a swift cloud”: after *hinnēh* the participle *rōḵēḇ* “riding, mounted” is a predicate, so the line has the present, “rides … and comes.” ASV and JPS 1917 have “rideth upon a swift cloud,” and NJPS has “Mounted on a swift cloud” (all checked). *ʿāḇ* is the dense mass of cloud (BDB). It is a different word from *ʿānān*, the general word for cloud at 4:5. English has “cloud” for both, so the Hebrew word is named here. *Qal* means “light,” and so “swift” (BDB), and the line keeps “swift” with all three versions. The Vulgate has *super nubem levem* “upon a light cloud,” and the Septuagint has *epi nephelēs kouphēs*, also “on a light cloud” (both recalled, not checked against an edition) (overlay `rokhev-al-av-qal-swift-cloud-isaiah-19`, new).

The image comes from the storm-theophany idiom of the Northwest Semitic world. In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle the storm-god Baʿlu has the standing epithet *rkb ʿrpt* “Rider of the Clouds.” The project's edition prints it at KTU 1.2 iv 6 (“did I not repeat (it) to you, O Rider of the Clouds?”), 1.3 ii 40, 1.3 iv 23 and 1.4 vi 10 (`BCY-WOH-1.2-iv:6` etc., checked). The Hebrew Bible applies the same image to YHWH: *rōḵēḇ bāʿărāḇôṯ* (Ps 68:5 [Eng. 4]), *rōḵēḇ šāmayim* (Deut 33:26), and “who makes the clouds (*ʿāḇîm*) his chariot” (Ps 104:3; cf. Ps 18:11). Cross (*Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic*, 1973) and Day (*Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan*, 2000) treat this as Baʿlu's imagery transferred to YHWH (as cited in the central entry; page references not re-checked). Isaiah does not use the epithet itself. The verse has a predicate participle, the singular *ʿāḇ* and the adjective *qal*, and no title. The line therefore translates a clause, in lower case, and does not print “Rider of the Clouds” (central `rider-of-the-clouds-rkb-arpt-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible-storm-theophany`, extended here). As the divine warrior arrives, the idols “tremble” (*nāʿû*, the verb of 6:4 and 7:2), and the heart of Egypt “melts” (*yimmas*, as at 13:7).

*Maśśāʾ miṣrāyim* is “The oracle concerning Egypt,” as at 13:1 and 15:1 (overlay `massa-oracle-superscription-isaiah`, extended here). *ʾĕlîlê miṣrayim* is “the idols of Egypt” (central `elilim-idols-cross-corpus`, whose wording already names 19:1 and 19:3). That entry records the play on *ʾēl* / *ʾĕlōhîm* and the sense “nothings,” which the line does not print.

**Wheel of Heaven reading (reception note, not a translation claim; claim type: speculative).** The canon does not cite Isa 19. *The Book Which Tells the Truth* reads two other biblical cloud passages as descriptions of craft. On 1 Kgs 8:12 it says: “That he dwells in a cloud — that is, in a craft in orbit around the Earth, above the clouds” (TBWTT 3:107). On Job 37:18 it speaks of “«solid clouds», in reality metallic flying craft” (TBWTT 3:259–260). Reading YHWH's “swift cloud” at Isa 19:1 in the same way extends those readings to a verse the canon does not discuss, so the reading is labelled speculative. The central rider-of-the-clouds entry records the scholarly position, that the image belongs to the storm-theophany idiom, and it rejects a vehicle reading of the Ugaritic epithet. The line and the glossary carry only the storm-theophany vocabulary.

paragraphs.translit: maśśāʾ miṣrāyim hinnēh YHWH rōkēb ʿal-ʿāb qal ūbāʾ miṣrayim wənāʿū ʾĕlīlē miṣrayim mippānāyw ūləbab miṣrayim yimmas bəqirbō

paragraphs.text: וְסִכְסַכְתִּ֤י מִצְרַ֙יִם֙ בְּמִצְרַ֔יִם וְנִלְחֲמ֥וּ אִישׁ־בְּאָחִ֖יו וְאִ֣ישׁ בְּרֵעֵ֑הוּ עִ֣יר בְּעִ֔יר מַמְלָכָ֖ה בְּמַמְלָכָֽה׃

i18n.en: And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they shall fight, everyone against his brother and everyone against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom.
i18n.he: וְסִכְסַכְתִּ֤י מִצְרַ֙יִם֙ בְּמִצְרַ֔יִם וְנִלְחֲמ֥וּ אִישׁ־בְּאָחִ֖יו וְאִ֣ישׁ בְּרֵעֵ֑הוּ עִ֣יר בְּעִ֔יר מַמְלָכָ֖ה בְּמַמְלָכָֽה׃

notes.official:
*Wᵉsiḵsaḵtî miṣrayim bᵉmiṣrayim* “I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians” follows ASV (“the Egyptians against the Egyptians”). JPS 1917 has “Egypt against Egypt,” and NJPS has “Egyptian against Egyptian” (all checked). The name *miṣrayim* means both the land and its people. Everywhere else in the chapter the line has “Egypt” where the Hebrew has the name, with the pronoun the Hebrew suffix or verb gives (“it,” “her,” “them”). ASV switches to “the Egyptians” at vv. 4, 16, 21 and 23. Only here does the line use “Egyptians,” because people fighting each other must be persons (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`, new).

*ʾîš bᵉʾāḥîw wᵉʾîš bᵉrēʿēhû* is distributive: “everyone against his brother and everyone against his neighbor” (ASV, JPS 1917). The generic *ʾîš* is “everyone,” as in the refrain of 2:9 and 5:15. The possessive “his” follows the Hebrew suffix, as at 9:18 and 13:8. An NJPS note explains *mamlāḵāh bᵉmamlāḵāh* “kingdom against kingdom” as the districts of Egypt, which in Isaiah's time were ruled by hereditary princes (checked).

paragraphs.translit: wəsiksaktī miṣrayim bəmiṣrayim wənilḥămū ʾīš-bəʾāḥīw wəʾīš bərēʿēhū ʿīr bəʿīr mamlākāh bəmamlākāh

paragraphs.text: וְנָבְקָ֤ה רֽוּחַ־מִצְרַ֙יִם֙ בְּקִרְבּ֔וֹ וַעֲצָת֖וֹ אֲבַלֵּ֑עַ וְדָרְשׁ֤וּ אֶל־הָֽאֱלִילִים֙ וְאֶל־הָ֣אִטִּ֔ים וְאֶל־הָאֹב֖וֹת וְאֶל־הַיִּדְּעֹנִֽים׃

i18n.en: And the spirit of Egypt shall be emptied within it, and I will destroy its counsel; and they shall seek the idols and the charmers, and the ghosts and the familiar spirits.
i18n.he: וְנָבְקָ֤ה רֽוּחַ־מִצְרַ֙יִם֙ בְּקִרְבּ֔וֹ וַעֲצָת֖וֹ אֲבַלֵּ֑עַ וְדָרְשׁ֤וּ אֶל־הָֽאֱלִילִים֙ וְאֶל־הָ֣אִטִּ֔ים וְאֶל־הָאֹב֖וֹת וְאֶל־הַיִּדְּעֹנִֽים׃

notes.official:
*Wᵉnāḇᵉqāh rûaḥ-miṣrayim* is the Niphal of *bqq* “empty out.” The line now has “shall be emptied” (JPS 1917 “shall be made empty”; NJPS “drained of spirit”) in place of the draft's “shall fail” (ASV). *Bqq* in the same stem is the verb of 24:3, “shall be utterly emptied.” “Fail” stays for a different verb, *nšt*, in v5 (“the waters shall fail”), so two Hebrew verbs in neighbouring verses no longer share one English word (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`). *Waʿăṣāṯô ʾăḇallēaʿ* “I will destroy its counsel” takes *blʿ* I “swallow” in the sense “bring to nothing,” as at 3:12 and 9:15 (“destroyed”). NJPS's “I will confound its plans” takes *blʿ* III “confuse” (HALOT). That alternative is recorded here, as it was at 3:12.

*Hāʾiṭṭîm* occurs only here. ASV “the charmers” and JPS 1917 “the whisperers” connect it with *ʾaṭ* “softly,” the low voice of the practitioner. HALOT compares Akkadian *eṭemmu* “spirit of a dead person” (recalled), and NJPS renders “the shades” (checked). The line keeps ASV. It does not use “shades,” because the book reserves that word for *rᵉp̄āʾîm* (14:9; 26:14, 19; overlay `rephaim-shades-dead-isaiah-26`), and “ghosts” already translates *ʾōḇôṯ* in the same list. *Hāʾōḇôṯ wᵉhayyiddᵉʿōnîm* are “the ghosts and the familiar spirits,” the spirits consulted, as at 8:19 (overlay `ob-yiddeoni-ghosts-familiar-spirits-isaiah`, extended here). JPS 1917 and NJPS use the same words. ASV renders practitioners: “them that have familiar spirits, and … the wizards” (checked). *Hāʾĕlîlîm* is “the idols” (central `elilim-idols-cross-corpus`).

paragraphs.translit: wənābəqāh rūaḥ-miṣrayim bəqirbō waʿăṣātō ʾăballēaʿ wədārəšū ʾel-hāʾĕlīlīm wəʾel-hāʾiṭṭīm wəʾel-hāʾōbōt wəʾel-hayyiddəʿōnīm

paragraphs.text: וְסִכַּרְתִּי֙ אֶת־מִצְרַ֔יִם בְּיַ֖ד אֲדֹנִ֣ים קָשֶׁ֑ה וּמֶ֤לֶךְ עַז֙ יִמְשָׁל־בָּ֔ם נְאֻ֥ם הָאָד֖וֹן יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: And I will give over Egypt into the hand of a cruel lord, and a fierce king shall rule over them, says the Sovereign, YHWH of hosts.
i18n.he: וְסִכַּרְתִּי֙ אֶת־מִצְרַ֔יִם בְּיַ֖ד אֲדֹנִ֣ים קָשֶׁ֑ה וּמֶ֤לֶךְ עַז֙ יִמְשָׁל־בָּ֔ם נְאֻ֥ם הָאָד֖וֹן יְהוָ֥ה צְבָאֽוֹת׃

notes.official:
*Bᵉyaḏ ʾăḏōnîm qāšeh* “into the hand of a cruel lord”: *ʾăḏōnîm* is plural in form, and the adjective is singular. The plural is used of a single master, as in *ʾăḏōnê hāʾāreṣ* “the lord of the land” for Joseph (Gen 42:30, 33). The line keeps ASV and JPS 1917 “a cruel lord.” NJPS has “a harsh master” (checked). The human *ʾăḏōnîm* and the divine title *hāʾāḏôn* at the end of the verse are the same noun. The English cannot show that with one word, because *hāʾāḏôn* is “the Sovereign” by house rule, so the repetition is noted here. The verse does not identify the cruel lord, who may be an Assyrian conqueror or a Kushite or Saite pharaoh, and the line does not decide.

*Nᵉʾum hāʾāḏôn YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* is “says the Sovereign, YHWH of hosts.” The title has the article, as at 1:24, 3:1 and 10:16, 33 (overlay `ha-adon-articular-title-isaiah`, whose wording already names 19:4 and which now lists it in its sites; NJPS “declares the Sovereign, the LORD of Hosts,” checked). *Nᵉʾum* is “says,” as at 14:22–23.

paragraphs.translit: wəsikkartī ʾet-miṣrayim bəyad ʾădōnīm qāšeh ūmelek ʿaz yimšol-bām nəʾum hāʾādōn YHWH ṣəbāʾōt

paragraphs.text: וְנִשְּׁתוּ־מַ֖יִם מֵֽהַיָּ֑ם וְנָהָ֖ר יֶחֱרַ֥ב וְיָבֵֽשׁ׃

i18n.en: And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and become dry.
i18n.he: וְנִשְּׁתוּ־מַ֖יִם מֵֽהַיָּ֑ם וְנָהָ֖ר יֶחֱרַ֥ב וְיָבֵֽשׁ׃

notes.official: *Wᵉniššᵉṯû-mayim mēhayyām* “And the waters shall fail from the sea”: *hayyām* “the sea” is the Nile, which Nah 3:8 also calls a sea. The line keeps the literal noun; NJPS has “the seas” (checked). *Wᵉnāhār* “and the river” is the common noun for a river, used here of the Nile in parallel with “the sea.” In Isaiah *hannāhār*, with the article and nothing further, is the Euphrates, and the line gives it a capital only there (“the River,” 7:20; 8:7; 11:15; 27:12). Under wave I-4 ruling 15 the Egyptian loanword *yᵉʾôr* is “the Nile” in vv. 7–8 (see 19:7). “The river” of v5 and “the Nile” of vv. 7–8 thus keep the two Hebrew words apart (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`). *Yeḥĕraḇ wᵉyāḇēš* is “shall be wasted and become dry” (ASV).

paragraphs.translit: wəniššətū-mayim mēhayyām wənāhār yeḥĕrab wəyābēš

paragraphs.text: וְהֶאֶזְנִ֣יחוּ נְהָר֔וֹת דָּלֲל֥וּ וְחָרְב֖וּ יְאֹרֵ֣י מָצ֑וֹר קָנֶ֥ה וָס֖וּף קָמֵֽלוּ׃

i18n.en: And the rivers shall become foul; the streams of Egypt shall dwindle and dry up; reed and rush shall wither.
i18n.he: וְהֶאֶזְנִ֣יחוּ נְהָר֔וֹת דָּלֲל֥וּ וְחָרְב֖וּ יְאֹרֵ֣י מָצ֑וֹר קָנֶ֥ה וָס֖וּף קָמֵֽלוּ׃

notes.official:
*Yᵉʾōrê māṣôr* “the streams of Egypt” (ASV, JPS 1917): the plural of *yᵉʾôr* means the branches and canals of the Nile (NJPS “Egypt's canals,” checked). At 7:18 the same plural is “the rivers of Egypt.” Here “rivers” already translates *nᵉhārôt* in the first colon, so the line keeps ASV's “streams” (wave I-4 ruling 15: plural *yᵉʾōrîm* “rivers/streams”; central `yeor-nile-egyptian-loanword`, extended here). *Māṣôr* is taken, with ASV, JPS 1917 and NJPS, as a poetic name for Egypt (cf. 37:25; 2 Kgs 19:24; Mic 7:12). Read as the common noun *māṣôr* “siege, fortification,” the phrase would be “the channels of the fortress.” “Egypt” in the line therefore stands for two Hebrew names, *miṣrayim* and *māṣôr*. The Koren edition transliterates “Mażor” (checked).

*Wᵉheʾeznîḥû* “shall become foul” (ASV; NJPS “turn foul”) is a Hiphil of *znḥ* found only here, with a prosthetic aleph (BDB). *Qāneh wāsûp̄* is “reed and rush.” *Sûp̄* is the reed of *yam-sûp̄*. The pair stands for the papyrus and reed beds of the Delta (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: wəheʾeznīḥū nəhārōt dālălū wəḥārəbū yəʾōrē māṣōr qāneh wāsūp qāmēlū

paragraphs.text: עָר֥וֹת עַל־יְא֖וֹר עַל־פִּ֣י יְא֑וֹר וְכֹל֙ מִזְרַ֣ע יְא֔וֹר יִיבַ֥שׁ נִדַּ֖ף וְאֵינֶֽנּוּ׃

i18n.en: The meadows by the Nile, by the brink of the Nile, and everything sown by the Nile shall dry up, be driven away, and be no more.
i18n.he: עָר֥וֹת עַל־יְא֖וֹר עַל־פִּ֣י יְא֑וֹר וְכֹל֙ מִזְרַ֣ע יְא֔וֹר יִיבַ֥שׁ נִדַּ֖ף וְאֵינֶֽנּוּ׃

notes.official:
*Yᵉʾôr* is “the Nile,” three times in this verse and once in v8. The draft had “the river,” the central default. ASV itself prints “the Nile” in these two verses, and so do JPS 1917 and NJPS (all checked). With the default, *yᵉʾôr* could not be told apart from *nāhār* “the river” in v5. Wave I-4 ruling 15 makes singular *yᵉʾôr* “the Nile” throughout Isaiah (central `yeor-nile-egyptian-loanword`, extended here; the context clause on that entry is carried with chapter 23). The central default “the river” stays in Gen 41.

*ʿĀrôṯ* occurs only here. ASV's “the meadows” derives it from *ʿrh* “be bare,” that is, open grassy places. JPS 1917 has “the mosses,” and NJPS has “the Nile papyrus,” with the note “Meaning of Heb. uncertain” (both checked). The line keeps ASV. *ʿAl-pî yᵉʾôr*, literally “at the mouth of the Nile,” means its edge, so the line has “by the brink of the Nile” (ASV, JPS 1917). The Koren edition's “by the mouth of the River” would suggest the Delta mouths. *Mizraʿ yᵉʾôr* is “everything sown by the Nile,” the fields watered by the flood (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: ʿārōt ʿal-yəʾōr ʿal-pī yəʾōr wəkōl mizraʿ yəʾōr yībaš niddap wəʾēnennū

paragraphs.text: וְאָנוּ֙ הַדַּיָּגִ֔ים וְאָ֣בְל֔וּ כָּל־מַשְׁלִיכֵ֥י בַיְא֖וֹר חַכָּ֑ה וּפֹרְשֵׂ֥י מִכְמֹ֛רֶת עַל־פְּנֵי־מַ֖יִם אֻמְלָֽלוּ׃

i18n.en: And the fishers shall lament, and all who cast a hook into the Nile shall mourn, and those who spread nets upon the waters shall languish.
i18n.he: וְאָנוּ֙ הַדַּיָּגִ֔ים וְאָ֣בְל֔וּ כָּל־מַשְׁלִיכֵ֥י בַיְא֖וֹר חַכָּ֑ה וּפֹרְשֵׂ֥י מִכְמֹ֛רֶת עַל־פְּנֵי־מַ֖יִם אֻמְלָֽלוּ׃

notes.official: *Mašlîḵê ḇayʾôr ḥakkāh* “who cast a hook into the Nile”: *ḥakkāh* is a fishhook (Job 40:25 [Eng. 41:1]), and ASV and JPS 1917 have “cast angle.” The fishers with hooks and the fishers with nets, followed by the flax workers of v9, are the Nile economy that fails with the water. For “the Nile,” see 19:7 (central `yeor-nile-egyptian-loanword`).

paragraphs.translit: wəʾānū haddayyāgīm wəʾābəlū kol-mašlīkē bayʾōr ḥakkāh ūpōrəśē mikmōret ʿal-pənē-mayim ʾumlālū

paragraphs.text: וּבֹ֛שׁוּ עֹבְדֵ֥י פִשְׁתִּ֖ים שְׂרִיק֑וֹת וְאֹרְגִ֖ים חוֹרָֽי׃

i18n.en: And those who work the combed flax and those who weave white cloth shall be ashamed.
i18n.he: וּבֹ֛שׁוּ עֹבְדֵ֥י פִשְׁתִּ֖ים שְׂרִיק֑וֹת וְאֹרְגִ֖ים חוֹרָֽי׃

notes.official: *Ḥôrāy* is rendered “white cloth” (ASV), from *ḥwr* “be white” (cf. *ḥûr* “white linen,” Esth 1:6; 8:15). JPS 1917 has “cotton.” NJPS reads the consonants as a verb, “(the weavers) chagrined,” with the note “Meaning of Heb. uncertain” (both checked). The line keeps the Masoretic vowels (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`, extended here). *Pištîm śᵉrîqôṯ* is “combed flax.” *Bōšû* is “shall be ashamed”; ASV has “confounded” (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: ūbōšū ʿōbədē pištīm śərīqōt wəʾōrəgīm ḥōrāy

paragraphs.text: וְהָי֥וּ שָׁתֹתֶ֖יהָ מְדֻכָּאִ֑ים כָּל־עֹ֥שֵׂי שֶׂ֖כֶר אַגְמֵי־נָֽפֶשׁ׃

i18n.en: And her pillars shall be crushed; all who work for hire shall be grieved in soul.
i18n.he: וְהָי֥וּ שָׁתֹתֶ֖יהָ מְדֻכָּאִ֑ים כָּל־עֹ֥שֵׂי שֶׂ֖כֶר אַגְמֵי־נָֽפֶשׁ׃

notes.official: NJPS marks the meaning of this verse as uncertain (checked). *Šāṯōṯêhā* “her pillars” (ASV; JPS 1917 and NJPS “her foundations”) is read from *šāṯ* “foundation” (Ps 11:3). MT *śeḵer* is “hire.” JPS 1917 and NJPS, “all who make dams,” read *sēḵer* “dam, weir.” *ʾAḡmê-nāp̄eš* is “grieved in soul” (cf. *ʿāḡᵉmāh nap̄šî* Job 30:25). NJPS reports an emendation: “Her drinkers shall be dejected, / And all her brewers despondent.” The line keeps MT (overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`, extended here). It drops ASV's supplied “[of Egypt]” and renders the suffix as “her” (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: wəhāyū šātōtēhā mədukkāʾīm kol-ʿōśē śeker ʾagmē-nāpeš

paragraphs.text: אַךְ־אֱוִלִים֙ שָׂ֣רֵי צֹ֔עַן חַכְמֵי֙ יֹעֲצֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔ה עֵצָ֖ה נִבְעָרָ֑ה אֵ֚יךְ תֹּאמְר֣וּ אֶל־פַּרְעֹ֔ה בֶּן־חֲכָמִ֥ים אֲנִ֖י בֶּן־מַלְכֵי־קֶֽדֶם׃

i18n.en: The princes of Zoan are utter fools; the counsel of the wisest counselors of Pharaoh has become brutish. How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings”?
i18n.he: אַךְ־אֱוִלִים֙ שָׂ֣רֵי צֹ֔עַן חַכְמֵי֙ יֹעֲצֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔ה עֵצָ֖ה נִבְעָרָ֑ה אֵ֚יךְ תֹּאמְר֣וּ אֶל־פַּרְעֹ֔ה בֶּן־חֲכָמִ֥ים אֲנִ֖י בֶּן־מַלְכֵי־קֶֽדֶם׃

notes.official: *Ḥaḵmê yōʿăṣê p̄arʿōh ʿēṣāh nibʿārāh* is literally “the wisest of Pharaoh's counselors: counsel has become brutish.” The line follows ASV's construal, “the counsel of the wisest counselors of Pharaoh has become brutish.” *ʿĒṣāh* is human counsel here and is “counsel” (see 19:17). *Ben-ḥăḵāmîm* is “a son of the wise,” where the plural is generic. *Ben-malḵê-qeḏem* is “a son of ancient kings” (ASV, JPS 1917). NJPS's “Kedemite kings” takes *qeḏem* as the East, whose wisdom was proverbial (1 Kgs 5:10 [Eng. 4:30]; checked) (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: ʾak-ʾĕwilīm śārē ṣōʿan ḥakmē yōʿăṣē parʿōh ʿēṣāh nibʿārāh ʾēk tōʾmərū ʾel-parʿōh ben-ḥăkāmīm ʾănī ben-malkē-qedem

paragraphs.text: אַיָּם֙ אֵפ֣וֹא חֲכָמֶ֔יךָ וְיַגִּ֥ידוּ נָ֖א לָ֑ךְ וְיֵ֣דְע֔וּ מַה־יָּעַ֛ץ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת עַל־מִצְרָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: Where, then, are your wise men? Let them tell you now, and let them know what YHWH of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt.
i18n.he: אַיָּם֙ אֵפ֣וֹא חֲכָמֶ֔יךָ וְיַגִּ֥ידוּ נָ֖א לָ֑ךְ וְיֵ֣דְע֔וּ מַה־יָּעַ֛ץ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת עַל־מִצְרָֽיִם׃

notes.official: *Ḥăḵāmêḵā* “your wise men” are Pharaoh's counselors of v11, the court class whose claim to wisdom the oracle mocks. The book's gender-neutral rule covers generic human nouns (overlay `adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah`). Under its scope ruling (wave I-4 ruling 13), nouns for specific male groups keep “men.” This noun names a specific body, the professional sages of Pharaoh's court. The line therefore keeps ASV and JPS 1917 “your wise men,” as the stable 29:14 has “the wisdom of its wise men.” NJPS has “your sages” (checked). *Yāʿaṣ* “has purposed” follows the stable 14:24, 26–27, where YHWH's plan is “purposed” and “the purpose” (see 19:17; overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: ʾayyām ʾēpōʾ ḥăkāmēkā wəyaggīdū nāʾ lāk wəyēdəʿū mah-yāʿaṣ YHWH ṣəbāʾōt ʿal-miṣrāyim

paragraphs.text: נֽוֹאֲלוּ֙ שָׂ֣רֵי צֹ֔עַן נִשְּׁא֖וּ שָׂ֣רֵי נֹ֑ף הִתְע֥וּ אֶת־מִצְרַ֖יִם פִּנַּ֥ת שְׁבָטֶֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: The princes of Zoan have become fools, the princes of Memphis are deceived; those who are the cornerstone of her tribes have led Egypt astray.
i18n.he: נֽוֹאֲלוּ֙ שָׂ֣רֵי צֹ֔עַן נִשְּׁא֖וּ שָׂ֣רֵי נֹ֑ף הִתְע֥וּ אֶת־מִצְרַ֖יִם פִּנַּ֥ת שְׁבָטֶֽיהָ׃

notes.official: *Pinnaṯ šᵉḇāṭêhā* “the cornerstone of her tribes” is in apposition to the subject. The princes, the leaders on whom the nation rests, have led Egypt astray (cf. *pinnôṯ kol-hāʿām* “the chiefs of all the people,” Judg 20:2). In the draft's word order the phrase read as if it described Egypt, so the line now follows ASV's construal: “those who are the cornerstone of her tribes have led Egypt astray” (ASV, JPS 1917 “that are the corner-stone of her tribes”; NJPS “by the chiefs of her tribes,” checked). *Nōp̄* is “Memphis” (ASV; wave I-4 ruling 4), where JPS 1917 transliterates “Noph.” *Ṣōʿan* is “Zoan” (ASV, JPS 1917), the Delta royal city that NJPS calls “Tanis” (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: nōʾălū śārē ṣōʿan niššəʾū śārē nōp hitʿū ʾet-miṣrayim pinnat šəbāṭēhā

paragraphs.text: יְהוָ֛ה מָסַ֥ךְ בְּקִרְבָּ֖הּ ר֣וּחַ עִוְעִ֑ים וְהִתְע֤וּ אֶת־מִצְרַ֙יִם֙ בְּכָֽל־מַעֲשֵׂ֔הוּ כְּהִתָּע֥וֹת שִׁכּ֖וֹר בְּקִיאֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: YHWH has mingled within her a spirit of perverseness; and they have led Egypt astray in all its work, as a drunkard staggers in his vomit.
i18n.he: יְהוָ֛ה מָסַ֥ךְ בְּקִרְבָּ֖הּ ר֣וּחַ עִוְעִ֑ים וְהִתְע֤וּ אֶת־מִצְרַ֙יִם֙ בְּכָֽל־מַעֲשֵׂ֔הוּ כְּהִתָּע֥וֹת שִׁכּ֖וֹר בְּקִיאֽוֹ׃

notes.official: *Rûaḥ ʿiwʿîm* is a plural found only here, from *ʿwh* “twist, distort.” ASV has “a spirit of perverseness,” JPS 1917 “a spirit of dizziness,” and NJPS “a spirit of distortion” (all checked). The line keeps ASV. This *rûaḥ* is a disposition that YHWH sends (cf. 29:10, “a spirit of deep sleep”), and it is lower case. The verb *tʿh* runs through vv. 13–14: the princes “led Egypt astray” (*hiṯʿû*, Hiphil), and the drunkard “staggers” (*kᵉhittāʿôṯ*, Hithpael) in his vomit. English cannot keep one word for both, and the play is noted here (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: YHWH māsak bəqirbāh rūaḥ ʿiwʿīm wəhitʿū ʾet-miṣrayim bəkāl-maʿăśēhū kəhittāʿōt šikkōr bəqīʾō

paragraphs.text: וְלֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֥ה לְמִצְרַ֖יִם מַֽעֲשֶׂ֑ה אֲשֶׁ֧ר יַעֲשֶׂ֛ה רֹ֥אשׁ וְזָנָ֖ב כִּפָּ֥ה וְאַגְמֽוֹן׃ (ס)

i18n.en: And there shall be no work for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or rush, can do.
i18n.he: וְלֹֽא־יִהְיֶ֥ה לְמִצְרַ֖יִם מַֽעֲשֶׂ֑ה אֲשֶׁ֧ר יַעֲשֶׂ֛ה רֹ֥אשׁ וְזָנָ֖ב כִּפָּ֥ה וְאַגְמֽוֹן׃ (ס)

notes.official: *Rōʾš wᵉzānāḇ kippāh wᵉʾaḡmôn* “head or tail, palm branch or rush” is the merism of 9:13 (“head and tail, palm branch and rush”). At 9:14 the book itself glosses it as the leaders and the false prophets, and an NJPS note here has “a man of either high or low station” (checked). The line keeps the nouns of 9:13.

paragraphs.translit: wəlōʾ-yihyeh ləmiṣrayim maʿăśeh ʾăšer yaʿăśeh rōʾš wəzānāb kippāh wəʾagmōn (s)

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא יִֽהְיֶ֥ה מִצְרַ֖יִם כַּנָּשִׁ֑ים וְחָרַ֣ד ׀ וּפָחַ֗ד מִפְּנֵי֙ תְּנוּפַת֙ יַד־יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֲשֶׁר־ה֖וּא מֵנִ֥יף עָלָֽיו׃

i18n.en: In that day Egypt shall be like women, and it shall tremble and fear because of the waving of the hand of YHWH of hosts, which he waves over it.
i18n.he: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא יִֽהְיֶ֥ה מִצְרַ֖יִם כַּנָּשִׁ֑ים וְחָרַ֣ד ׀ וּפָחַ֗ד מִפְּנֵי֙ תְּנוּפַת֙ יַד־יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֲשֶׁר־ה֖וּא מֵנִ֥יף עָלָֽיו׃

notes.official: *Tᵉnûp̄aṯ yaḏ-YHWH … ʾăšer-hûʾ mēnîp̄ ʿālāyw* “the waving of the hand … which he waves over it”: the Hiphil of *nûp̄* with *yāḏ* is the brandished hand, the same verb as *hēnîp̄ yāḏô* “he will wave his hand” at 11:15. ASV and JPS 1917 have “shaking … shaketh,” and NJPS has “will raise His hand against them” (all checked). The line keeps one English verb for the gesture at both sites. The cultic noun *tᵉnûp̄āh* “wave-offering” (central `qorbanot-sacrificial-offering-vocabulary-cluster-cross-corpus`) is not meant here, and that entry is not applied to this verse. *Kannāšîm* “like women” is the simile for a force that loses its nerve (cf. Jer 50:37; 51:30; Nah 3:13), and it is rendered literally (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: bayyōm hahūʾ yihyeh miṣrayim kannāšīm wəḥārad | ūpāḥad mippənē tənūpat yad-YHWH ṣəbāʾōt ʾăšer-hūʾ mēnīp ʿālāyw

paragraphs.text: וְ֠הָיְתָה אַדְמַ֨ת יְהוּדָ֤ה לְמִצְרַ֙יִם֙ לְחָגָּ֔א כֹּל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יַזְכִּ֥יר אֹתָ֛הּ אֵלָ֖יו יִפְחָ֑ד מִפְּנֵ֗י עֲצַת֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֲשֶׁר־ה֖וּא יוֹעֵ֥ץ עָלָֽיו׃ (ס)

i18n.en: And the ground of Judah shall become a terror to Egypt; everyone to whom it is mentioned shall fear, because of the purpose of YHWH of hosts, which he purposes against it.
i18n.he: וְ֠הָיְתָה אַדְמַ֨ת יְהוּדָ֤ה לְמִצְרַ֙יִם֙ לְחָגָּ֔א כֹּל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יַזְכִּ֥יר אֹתָ֛הּ אֵלָ֖יו יִפְחָ֑ד מִפְּנֵ֗י עֲצַת֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֲשֶׁר־ה֖וּא יוֹעֵ֥ץ עָלָֽיו׃ (ס)

notes.official:
*ʾAḏmaṯ yᵉhûḏāh* “the ground of Judah”: the book renders *ʾăḏāmāh* “ground” throughout (14:1 “their own ground”; 14:2 “the ground of YHWH”; 32:13 “the ground of my people”; central `adam-adamah`, extended here). *ʾEreṣ* is “land” in the verses that follow (vv. 18–20). ASV, JPS 1917 and NJPS have “the land of Judah” (checked). *Lᵉḥāggāʾ* “a terror” is a noun found only here; ASV and JPS 1917 have “a terror,” and NJPS has “the dread.” *Kōl ʾăšer yazkîr ʾōṯāh ʾēlāyw yip̄ḥāḏ* is construed with ASV: “everyone to whom it is mentioned shall fear.” NJPS reads an indefinite subject, “they shall quake whenever anybody mentions it to them” (checked).

For the *ʿēṣāh* / *yāʿaṣ* pair, the line follows ASV: “purpose … purposes” where YHWH plans (vv. 12, 17, as in the stable 14:24–27), and “counsel” for the advice of human counselors (vv. 3, 11). One Hebrew root thus has two English words. The book had already made this choice, and the shift follows the speaker (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: wəhāyətāh ʾadmat yəhūdāh ləmiṣrayim ləḥāggāʾ kōl ʾăšer yazkīr ʾōtāh ʾēlāyw yipḥād mippənē ʿăṣat YHWH ṣəbāʾōt ʾăšer-hūʾ yōʿēṣ ʿālāyw (s)

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֡וּא יִהְיוּ֩ חָמֵ֨שׁ עָרִ֜ים בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֗יִם מְדַבְּרוֹת֙ שְׂפַ֣ת כְּנַ֔עַן וְנִשְׁבָּע֖וֹת לַיהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת עִ֣יר הַהֶ֔רֶס יֵאָמֵ֖ר לְאֶחָֽת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear to YHWH of hosts; one shall be called the City of Destruction.
i18n.he: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֡וּא יִהְיוּ֩ חָמֵ֨שׁ עָרִ֜ים בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֗יִם מְדַבְּרוֹת֙ שְׂפַ֣ת כְּנַ֔עַן וְנִשְׁבָּע֖וֹת לַיהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת עִ֣יר הַהֶ֔רֶס יֵאָמֵ֖ר לְאֶחָֽת׃ (ס)

notes.official:
*ʿÎr haheres* “the City of Destruction” follows the Masoretic Text, with ASV and JPS 1917 (checked; wave I-4 ruling 5; overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`, extended here, and `ir-haheres-city-of-destruction-isaiah-19`, new). *Heres* “destruction” is a noun from *hrs* “tear down” that occurs only here. Many Hebrew manuscripts read *ḥeres* “sun” (NJPS note, checked). The same reading is reported for the Great Isaiah Scroll, 1QIsaᵃ (not checked against the DJD edition). “City of the Sun” would be Heliopolis, the Hebrew On (central `on-heliopolis-egyptian-toponym`), which Jer 43:13 calls *bêṯ šemeš* “the house of the sun.” The NJPS note records the manuscript reading and the Targum's “Beth Shemesh,” and NJPS itself prints “Town of Heres” (checked). The Vulgate has *civitas Solis* “city of the Sun,” and the Septuagint has *polis asedek*, as if *ʿîr haṣṣedeq* “city of righteousness” (cf. 1:26) (both recalled, not checked against an edition). Commentators often explain MT *haheres* as a deliberate change from *haḥeres*, made in reaction to the Jewish temple in the Heliopolite district (see 19:19). Others hold that MT is original (Wildberger; Blenkinsopp; not re-checked). The line does not decide between them.

*Śᵉp̄aṯ kᵉnaʿan* is literally “the lip of Canaan,” the language of Canaan, that is, Hebrew. ASV, JPS 1917 and NJPS have “the language of Canaan” (checked). The central `safa-achat-devarim-achadim` entry keeps “lip” at Gen 11:1, where the doubled noun phrase is the point. That rule is not extended here, and the entry is not applied. *Ḥāmēš ʿārîm* is “five cities.” NJPS prints “several,” with the note “Lit. ‘five,’” and it renders *lᵉʾeḥāṯ* “one,” with the note “Or ‘each one’” (checked). *Wᵉnišbāʿôṯ laYHWH* “and swear to YHWH” is an oath of allegiance (NJPS “swearing loyalty”). *ʾEreṣ miṣrayim* is a territory and is “the land of Egypt” (central `eretz`).

paragraphs.translit: bayyōm hahūʾ yihyū ḥāmēš ʿārīm bəʾereṣ miṣrayim mədabbərōt śəpat kənaʿan wənišbāʿōt laYHWH ṣəbāʾōt ʿīr haheres yēʾāmēr ləʾeḥāt (s)

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא יִֽהְיֶ֤ה מִזְבֵּ֙חַ֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה בְּת֖וֹךְ אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרָ֑יִם וּמַצֵּבָ֥ה אֵֽצֶל־גְּבוּלָ֖הּ לַֽיהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: In that day there shall be an altar to YHWH in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to YHWH at its border.
i18n.he: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא יִֽהְיֶ֤ה מִזְבֵּ֙חַ֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה בְּת֖וֹךְ אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרָ֑יִם וּמַצֵּבָ֥ה אֵֽצֶל־גְּבוּלָ֖הּ לַֽיהוָֽה׃

notes.official:
*Mizbēaḥ laYHWH bᵉṯôḵ ʾereṣ miṣrāyim ûmaṣṣēḇāh … laYHWH* is “an altar to YHWH in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to YHWH at its border.” The nouns are the plain “altar” and “pillar” (central `mizbeach-olah` and `matzevah-sacred-pillar-patriarchal-religion`, both extended here). A *maṣṣēḇāh* is a sacred standing stone. Deuteronomic law forbids setting one up for YHWH (Deut 16:22), while the patriarchal narratives record such stones without censure (Gen 28:18, 22; 35:14). Here the oracle assigns one to YHWH at the border of Egypt. An NJPS note explains it “As a symbol of the Lord’s sovereignty over Egypt” (checked). The line renders the nouns and does not smooth over the tension with Deut 16:22. *ʾEreṣ miṣrāyim* is “the land of Egypt” (central `eretz`).

**Reception.** Josephus reports that the priest Onias IV built a temple at Leontopolis, in the Heliopolite district, in the second century BCE. Onias defended the temple by citing this prophecy of Isaiah (*Antiquities* 13.62–73; *War* 7.420–436; recalled, section numbers not re-checked). The Mishnah rules on vows and priests connected with “the house of Onias” (m. Menaḥ. 13:10; recalled). This history is often proposed as the setting of the variants in v18. It is reported here as reception and does not affect the line (wave I-4 ruling 5).

paragraphs.translit: bayyōm hahūʾ yihyeh mizbēaḥ laYHWH bətōk ʾereṣ miṣrāyim ūmaṣṣēbāh ʾēṣel-gəbūlāh laYHWH

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָ֨ה לְא֥וֹת וּלְעֵ֛ד לַֽיהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרָ֑יִם כִּֽי־יִצְעֲק֤וּ אֶל־יְהוָה֙ מִפְּנֵ֣י לֹֽחֲצִ֔ים וְיִשְׁלַ֥ח לָהֶ֛ם מוֹשִׁ֥יעַ וָרָ֖ב וְהִצִּילָֽם׃

i18n.en: And it shall be for a sign and for a witness to YHWH of hosts in the land of Egypt; for they shall cry to YHWH because of oppressors, and he will send them a savior and a defender, and he will deliver them.
i18n.he: וְהָיָ֨ה לְא֥וֹת וּלְעֵ֛ד לַֽיהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת בְּאֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרָ֑יִם כִּֽי־יִצְעֲק֤וּ אֶל־יְהוָה֙ מִפְּנֵ֣י לֹֽחֲצִ֔ים וְיִשְׁלַ֥ח לָהֶ֛ם מוֹשִׁ֥יעַ וָרָ֖ב וְהִצִּילָֽם׃

notes.official: *Wᵉhāyāh lᵉʾôṯ ûlᵉʿēḏ* “And it shall be for a sign and for a witness”: the subject is the altar and pillar of v19 taken together. ASV and JPS 1917 have “it,” and NJPS has “They shall serve as a symbol and reminder” (checked). *Mōšîaʿ wārāḇ* is “a savior and a defender” (ASV, JPS 1917; NJPS “a savior and champion,” checked). This takes *rāḇ* as the participle of *rîḇ* “contend, plead a cause.” KJV reads the adjective: “a saviour, and a great one” (recalled). The line follows ASV. “Savior” is lower case and unqualified. The verse uses the deliverer pattern of Judges (*wayyizʿăqû … wayyāqem YHWH môšîaʿ*, Judg 3:9, 15), with Egypt in Israel's place. Attempts to identify the deliverer belong to reception history, and the line makes none (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`). *ʾEreṣ miṣrāyim* is “the land of Egypt” (central `eretz`).

paragraphs.translit: wəhāyāh ləʾōt ūləʿēd laYHWH ṣəbāʾōt bəʾereṣ miṣrāyim kī-yiṣʿăqū ʾel-YHWH mippənē lōḥăṣīm wəyišlaḥ lāhem mōšīaʿ wārāb wəhiṣṣīlām

paragraphs.text: וְנוֹדַ֤ע יְהוָה֙ לְמִצְרַ֔יִם וְיָדְע֥וּ מִצְרַ֛יִם אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וְעָֽבְדוּ֙ זֶ֣בַח וּמִנְחָ֔ה וְנָדְרוּ־נֵ֥דֶר לַֽיהוָ֖ה וְשִׁלֵּֽמוּ׃

i18n.en: And YHWH shall be known to Egypt, and Egypt shall know YHWH in that day; and they shall worship with sacrifice and meal-offering, and shall vow a vow to YHWH and fulfill it.
i18n.he: וְנוֹדַ֤ע יְהוָה֙ לְמִצְרַ֔יִם וְיָדְע֥וּ מִצְרַ֛יִם אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וְעָֽבְדוּ֙ זֶ֣בַח וּמִנְחָ֔ה וְנָדְרוּ־נֵ֥דֶר לַֽיהוָ֖ה וְשִׁלֵּֽמוּ׃

notes.official: *Wᵉnôḏaʿ YHWH lᵉmiṣrayim* “And YHWH shall be known to Egypt” renders the Niphal as a passive, with ASV. JPS 1917 and NJPS take it as reflexive: “the LORD shall make Himself known” (checked). Both readings are grammatical. In *wᵉʿāḇᵉḏû zeḇaḥ ûminḥāh*, *ʿāḇaḏ* with the offering as its object means serving God by means of sacrifice. The line keeps ASV and JPS 1917 “worship with sacrifice,” and NJPS has “they shall serve [Him] with sacrifice and oblation” (checked). In a cultic pair, *zeḇaḥ* and *minḥāh* are “sacrifice and meal-offering” (central `qorbanot-sacrificial-offering-vocabulary-cluster-cross-corpus`, extended here; ASV “oblation”). *Wᵉnāḏᵉrû-nēḏer … wᵉšillēmû* “and shall vow a vow … and fulfill it” keeps the cognate object (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: wənōdaʿ YHWH ləmiṣrayim wəyādəʿū miṣrayim ʾet-YHWH bayyōm hahūʾ wəʿābədū zebaḥ ūminḥāh wənādərū-nēder laYHWH wəšillēmū

paragraphs.text: וְנָגַ֧ף יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־מִצְרַ֖יִם נָגֹ֣ף וְרָפ֑וֹא וְשָׁ֙בוּ֙ עַד־יְהוָ֔ה וְנֶעְתַּ֥ר לָהֶ֖ם וּרְפָאָֽם׃

i18n.en: And YHWH will strike Egypt, striking and healing; and they shall return to YHWH, and he will be entreated by them and will heal them.
i18n.he: וְנָגַ֧ף יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־מִצְרַ֖יִם נָגֹ֣ף וְרָפ֑וֹא וְשָׁ֙בוּ֙ עַד־יְהוָ֔ה וְנֶעְתַּ֥ר לָהֶ֖ם וּרְפָאָֽם׃

notes.official: *Nāḡōp̄ wᵉrāp̄ôʾ* are two infinitives absolute after the finite verb: “striking and healing” (ASV, JPS 1917). NJPS makes the sequence explicit, “will first afflict and then heal” (checked). *Wᵉneʿtar lāhem* “he will be entreated by them” is the tolerative Niphal of *ʿtr*, “let himself be moved by prayer.” The verse repeats the pattern of v20, in which the people cry out and YHWH answers.

paragraphs.translit: wənāgap YHWH ʾet-miṣrayim nāgōp wərāpōʾ wəšābū ʿad-YHWH wəneʿtar lāhem ūrəpāʾām

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא תִּהְיֶ֨ה מְסִלָּ֤ה מִמִּצְרַ֙יִם֙ אַשּׁ֔וּרָה וּבָֽא־אַשּׁ֥וּר בְּמִצְרַ֖יִם וּמִצְרַ֣יִם בְּאַשּׁ֑וּר וְעָבְד֥וּ מִצְרַ֖יִם אֶת־אַשּֽׁוּר׃ (ס)

i18n.en: In that day there shall be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria shall come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria; and Egypt shall worship with Assyria.
i18n.he: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא תִּהְיֶ֨ה מְסִלָּ֤ה מִמִּצְרַ֙יִם֙ אַשּׁ֔וּרָה וּבָֽא־אַשּׁ֥וּר בְּמִצְרַ֖יִם וּמִצְרַ֣יִם בְּאַשּׁ֑וּר וְעָבְד֥וּ מִצְרַ֖יִם אֶת־אַשּֽׁוּר׃ (ס)

notes.official: *Mᵉsillāh* “a highway” is a built-up road, as at 11:16 and 40:3. In *wᵉʿāḇᵉḏû miṣrayim ʾeṯ-ʾaššûr*, *ʾeṯ* is taken as the preposition “with”: “Egypt shall worship with Assyria” (ASV, JPS 1917; NJPS “the Egyptians together with the Assyrians shall serve [the LORD],” checked). Taken as the object marker, the clause would mean “Egypt shall serve Assyria,” and vv. 21 and 24–25 do not favour that reading. The line keeps the names where ASV has “the Assyrian … the Egyptian” (see 19:2; overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: bayyōm hahūʾ tihyeh məsillāh mimmiṣrayim ʾaššūrāh ūbāʾ-ʾaššūr bəmiṣrayim ūmiṣrayim bəʾaššūr wəʿābədū miṣrayim ʾet-ʾaššūr (s)

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא יִהְיֶ֤ה יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ שְׁלִ֣ישִׁיָּ֔ה לְמִצְרַ֖יִם וּלְאַשּׁ֑וּר בְּרָכָ֖ה בְּקֶ֥רֶב הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: In that day Israel shall be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth,
i18n.he: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא יִהְיֶ֤ה יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ שְׁלִ֣ישִׁיָּ֔ה לְמִצְרַ֖יִם וּלְאַשּׁ֑וּר בְּרָכָ֖ה בְּקֶ֥רֶב הָאָֽרֶץ׃

notes.official:
*Bᵉqereḇ hāʾāreṣ* is “in the midst of the earth” (ASV, JPS 1917; NJPS “on earth,” checked). The central default for *ʾereṣ* is “land.” The overlay `eretz-cosmic-scope-isaiah-24`, extended here, gives “earth” where the horizon is universal, and a blessing that joins Egypt, Assyria and Israel has that horizon. The Koren edition renders “in the midst of the land” (checked), which would point to the territory between the two powers. That reading is recorded but not adopted. In vv. 18–20, *ʾereṣ miṣrāyim* is a territory and is “the land of Egypt” (central `eretz`).

*Šᵉlîšiyyāh* is “the third” (ASV, JPS 1917); NJPS has “a third partner.” *Bᵉrāḵāh* “a blessing” recalls the promise to Abraham, “and be a blessing” (Gen 12:2). An NJPS note makes the same link and explains the noun as “a standard by which blessing is invoked” (checked) (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

paragraphs.translit: bayyōm hahūʾ yihyeh yiśrāʾēl šəlīšiyyāh ləmiṣrayim ūləʾaššūr bərākāh bəqereb hāʾāreṣ

paragraphs.text: אֲשֶׁ֧ר בֵּרֲכ֛וֹ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת לֵאמֹ֑ר בָּר֨וּךְ עַמִּ֜י מִצְרַ֗יִם וּמַעֲשֵׂ֤ה יָדַי֙ אַשּׁ֔וּר וְנַחֲלָתִ֖י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ (ס)

i18n.en: whom YHWH of hosts has blessed, saying, “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.”
i18n.he: אֲשֶׁ֧ר בֵּרֲכ֛וֹ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת לֵאמֹ֑ר בָּר֨וּךְ עַמִּ֜י מִצְרַ֗יִם וּמַעֲשֵׂ֤ה יָדַי֙ אַשּׁ֔וּר וְנַחֲלָתִ֖י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ (ס)

notes.official:
*ʾĂšer bērăḵô YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* has a singular suffix: “whom … has blessed.” The line takes *ʾăšer* as a relative pronoun. Its referent is Israel, the nearest person named, or the three nations taken as one, and Koren also has “whom.” ASV and JPS 1917 take *ʾăšer* as causal (“for that”). ASV supplies the plural “them,” JPS 1917 keeps the singular “him,” and NJPS has the future “for the LORD of Hosts will bless them” (all checked). *Bārûḵ* is the formula of wish, “Blessed be.” The Hebrew order is *bārûḵ ʿammî miṣrayim ûmaʿăśēh yāḏay ʾaššûr wᵉnaḥălāṯî yiśrāʾēl*, “Blessed be my people Egypt, and the work of my hands Assyria, and my inheritance Israel.” NJPS follows that order. The line keeps ASV's order, “Egypt my people.” Elsewhere all three epithets are Israel's own: “my people” (1:3), “the work of my hands” (60:21; cf. 64:7 [Eng. 8]) and “my inheritance” (47:6) (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-19`).

**Reception.** The Septuagint renders the blessing “Blessed be my people who are in Egypt and who are among the Assyrians, and my inheritance Israel.” In that version Egypt and Assyria become places of the Jewish diaspora, not nations blessed as peoples (recalled, not checked against an edition). The Hebrew line keeps the nations as the ones blessed. Later universalist and Christian readings of vv. 19–25 are reception history and do not affect the line (wave I-4 ruling 5).

paragraphs.translit: ʾăšer bērăkō YHWH ṣəbāʾōt lēʾmōr bārūk ʿammī miṣrayim ūmaʿăśēh yāday ʾaššūr wənaḥălātī yiśrāʾēl (s)
